slides.title: Device Sign-In
slides.subtitle: Sign in on the company's page when the agent cannot take a browser callback
slides.notes: Some personal agents run in a terminal or on a device with no browser callback. Device Sign-In lets the user sign in on the company's page with a link and a code, while the agent polls politely for the result.

slides.title: Why Device Sign-In
slides.statement: The user signs in **elsewhere**. The agent **waits**, at the company's pace.
slides.notes: The user opens a link on any device and types a short code. Meanwhile the agent asks the company whether sign-in is done, never faster than the company allows.

slides.title: Who takes part

columns.heading: Agent tool
columns.content: A read-only tool. Shows the user the **link and code**.

columns.heading: DeviceSignInClient
columns.content: The real SDK state machine. Polls with **DPoP**, keeps the device code private.

columns.heading: Company and Reactor
columns.content: The company signs the user in; **Reactor** stores hold the device code and the Account Token.

slides.notes: The tool only presents what the user needs. The SDK client runs the state machine against a deterministic company transport, and Reactor stores keep the secrets: the device code, and later the Account Token.

slides.title: Starting

items.title: Authorize
items.detail: Link, user code, interval, private device code

items.title: Hand off
items.detail: The user opens the link and enters the code

slides.notes: The client asks the company for a device authorization on the Session that already exists. The company returns a link, a user code, a polling interval and a private device code. The device code goes into a Reactor store; the tool gets the link, the code and an opaque reference.

slides.title: Polling at the company's pace

items.title: Too early
items.detail: No request: the interval has not passed

items.title: Signed in
items.detail: Same Session, Account Token, partial scopes

slides.notes: A poll before the interval sends nothing. Then the company says pending, then slow down, and the client adds five seconds to its interval. Every poll that goes out carries a fresh DPoP proof. Finally the same Session comes back signed in, with an Account Token and one requested scope missing.

slides.title: What the example proves
items: The link and the code were shown to the user
One requested scope was left out, and reported
slides.notes: The tool result is a list of evidence like this. It shows the polling rules held and that the Session was upgraded rather than replaced.

slides.title: What stays where

right.heading: What the model sees
items: The link and user code, as shown

slides.notes: The user code is meant for the user; the device code is not, and never leaves the host. Tokens, assertions and proofs stay host-only too.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples run the real state machine against a deterministic company
slides.notes: The company in the examples always answers pending, then slow down, so every rule is exercised on each run. The Device Sign-In guide covers the production setup.
